files.name: WebhookService.cs

notes.6: A shared HttpClient instance (reuse is the recommended pattern).
notes.9: `webhookUrl` is configured by the customer — attacker-controlled.
notes.11: Wraps the event JSON as the request body.
notes.12: The server POSTs to that URL.
notes.13: Returns the response body to the caller.

options.label: A static HttpClient leaks sockets and should be disposed per call
options.whyWrong: Reusing HttpClient is actually correct; this isn't the security issue.

options.label: StringContent defaults to text/plain, which some servers reject
options.whyWrong: A content-type nit has nothing to do with the vulnerability.

options.label: `webhookUrl` is user-configured and the request is made by the server, so it can reach internal-only endpoints; returning the body leaks their contents
Require the URL to use https
options.whyWrong: `https://169.254.169.254` or an internal HTTPS service is still reachable; scheme isn't the control.

options.label: Allow only http/https, resolve the host, and reject private/loopback/link-local addresses (re-checking on redirects)
Add a request timeout
options.whyWrong: A timeout limits how long the request runs, not where it goes.

options.label: Reject URLs containing 'internal' or 'localhost'
options.whyWrong: IP literals and other hostnames bypass the substring check.

training.exploit: A customer sets their webhook URL to `http://169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data/iam/security-credentials/` (cloud metadata) or `http://127.0.0.1:8500/v1/kv/?recurse` (internal Consul). The server dutifully requests it and returns the response body — handing the attacker internal data or credentials.

hints.line: Where does the server fetch a URL it was handed?
hints.bugClass: The server reaches a destination the user chose.
hints.why: What internal hosts can the server reach that the customer can't?
hints.fix: Validate the resolved destination is a public address you intend.

writeup.summary: `Deliver` POSTs to any URL the customer configured and returns the response, from the server's privileged network position — textbook SSRF. An attacker points the webhook at cloud metadata or internal services to exfiltrate credentials and data. The fix validates the scheme, resolves the host, and rejects private/loopback/link-local ranges (re-checking after any redirect), rather than blocklisting hostnames or relying on https.
